title: Transient Information
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: This is the fifth edition of Jamie Clark's Cognitive Load Theory series for teachers, and it explains why spoken instructions, moving slides, videos and rubbed-out board work vanish before students have finished processing them. Clark defines transient information and clarifies what it is not: it is not a ban on teacher talk, an argument against video, or something fixed by slowing down. He cites studies in which Year 6 students scored 43% reading long explanations against 23% hearing them, and in which splitting a spoken explanation into short chunks with pauses helped listeners. He adds the caveat that these studies used recorded narration rather than live teachers who can pause and check understanding. Using Oliver Caviglioli's idea of the board as an external memory field, he offers five practical steps: write down what students must keep, say one step at a time, leave every step visible, chop videos into short clips, and tell students to go back to the written version. The edition is a research-grounded, classroom-ready translation of CLT rather than a theory piece.
points: Transient information is anything that disappears before students have processed it, such as speech, moving slides, video and erased board work, and it bites hardest when students must hold one idea in mind to understand the next.
In the cited graph-reading study, long explanations flipped the usual spoken advantage: readers scored 43% and listeners 23% on identical content, so length rather than modality was the problem.
Chunking helps: a two-minute spoken explanation split into eight short pieces with five-second pauses improved listeners' test and transfer results.
Written information only helps if students return to it, so teachers need to prompt re-reading before work starts and again when students get stuck.
The five fixes all make the important things stay visible, for example numbering the six steps of a practical on the board and leaving them up throughout.
quotes: Transient information is information that disappears before students have finished processing it. The most common example is speech: once we’ve said something, it's instantly gone, unless students hold it in their working memory.
In the classroom, however, it becomes more challenging because students must hold earlier information in mind to make sense of what comes next.

When the explanations came in short statements, the spoken version won. When the same content came in long statements, the result flipped: students who read it scored 43%, and students who heard it scored 23%. The content was identical, it was only the length that changed.
But when the spoken version was split into eight short chunks, with a five-second pause after each, listeners improved on both.
In other words, having information available is only useful if students actually make use of it.
When students need to hold several pieces of information in mind at once, anything we communicate only verbally places additional demands on their limited working memory.
Make information visible to help free-up working memory. When it’s short and simple, say it. When it’s long and complex, write it and leave it up.
Writing things down only helps if students return to it. Prompt them to re-read before they start, and again when they get stuck.

Before the lesson begins, the six steps are numbered on the board. The teacher talks through each one, pointing to it as they go, before modelling the first step with the equipment. The instructions remain up and visible throughout the practical, giving students something to refer back to whenever they need it.
